title: We receive dogmas because God revealed them; arguments persuade, revelation grounds; 1 Peter 3
source_text: XXV. Nam quod attinet ad res ipsas quae traduntur in Dei verbo, ut sunt quae vocantur fidei dogmata, et alia quae habentur in Scripturis, illis assentimur, eaque ut vera recipimus, quoniam Deus, qui est summe verax, quique nec falli, nec fallere potest, illa per Apostolos et Prophetas nobis revelavit, et in verbo suo docuit. Habent quidem fidei dogmata, praeter divinam revelationem, argumenta multa quibus probentur et suadentur. Neque solet Deus nos ad eorum fidem adducere, nisi mediantibus quibusdam argumentis, indiciis et rationibus, quibus eorum veritas menti nostrae credibilis redditur, et suaviter in animos nostros insinuatur. Unde est quod Petrus 1. Epist. cap. 3. vult ut fideles possint defensione uti, et satisfacere cuivis petenti rationem ejus quae in ipsis est spei. Qui vero absque omni ratione crederet, nec fidei suae rationem ullam haberet, aut reddere posset, ista non esset vera fides, sed levis et temeraria quaedam persuasio. Ideoque non sufficit iis, qui verbum Dei annuntiant, simpliciter doctrinam fidei proponere, sed praeterea opus est, ut suasiones quasdam adhibeant, et vel ex ipsis rebus, vel ex quibusdam adjunctis argumenta eliciant, quibus religionis Christianae mysteria credibilia reddant, et etiam valide comprobent. Attamen fidei nostrae praecipuum fundamentum, et propria ratio, non sunt illae qualescunque rationes et argumenta, sed divina revelatio, in quam praesertim fides nostra recumbit.
pass_a_gloss: For as for the things themselves which are handed down in God's Word, such as those called dogmas of faith, and other things held in the Scriptures, we assent to them, and receive them as true, because God, who is supremely truthful, and who can neither be deceived nor deceive, revealed them to us through Apostles and Prophets, and taught them in his Word. The dogmas of faith do indeed have, besides divine revelation, many arguments by which they are proved and urged. Nor does God ordinarily lead us to faith in them except through certain mediating arguments, indications, and reasons, by which their truth is made credible to our mind, and gently is worked into our souls. Whence it is that Peter in the first Epistle, chapter 3, wills that believers be able to use a defense, and to satisfy anyone asking a reason of the hope that is in them. But whoever would believe without any reason, and would have no reason of his faith, or could not give one, that would not be true faith, but a light and rash certain persuasion. And therefore it is not enough for those who announce God's Word simply to propose the doctrine of faith; besides that there is need that they apply certain persuasions, and draw out arguments either from the things themselves or from certain adjuncts, by which they make the mysteries of the Christian religion credible, and also strongly prove them. Nevertheless the principal foundation of our faith, and its proper ground, are not those reasons and arguments of whatever kind, but divine revelation, on which our faith especially rests.
pass_b_english: As for the things themselves handed down in God's Word — the so-called dogmas of faith, and the other things held in the Scriptures — we assent to them and receive them as true because God, who is supremely truthful and can neither be deceived nor deceive, revealed them to us through Apostles and Prophets and taught them in his Word. Besides divine revelation, the dogmas of faith do have many arguments by which they are proved and urged. God does not ordinarily lead us to faith in them except through mediating arguments, indications, and reasons that make their truth credible to our mind and gently work it into our souls.

That is why Peter wills that believers be able to give a defense, and to satisfy anyone who asks a reason for the hope that is in them (1 Peter 3). Whoever would believe with no reason at all, and would have no account of his faith or could not give one, would not have true faith, only a light and rash persuasion. So those who announce God's Word must not merely propose the doctrine of faith. They also need to apply persuasions and draw arguments from the things themselves or from adjuncts, so as to make the mysteries of the Christian religion credible and even strongly prove them. Still, the principal foundation of our faith, and its proper ground, is not those reasons and arguments of whatever kind, but divine revelation, on which our faith especially rests.
